# Part IV. Strategic and Social Decisions {.unnumbered}

A team would benefit if everyone shared what they knew. Yet a member may stay quiet because speaking first seems risky, because others appear certain, or because the person who challenges the group usually pays a cost. A warning can disappear from the discussion while everyone takes the silence as agreement. The same silence can arise for different reasons; how can the team discover which one it needs to address?

The route in @fig-part-4-route starts with strategic dependence: what makes sense for one person depends on what others may do. We then ask why people cooperate, punish, follow norms, and learn from one another. Markets provide a larger setting in which individual forecasts become prices and those prices become information for later decisions.

The final chapters return to the problem of interpreting agreement. Authority may discourage a challenge, group discussion may leave unique information unshared, and culture or identity may change what silence means. These explanations call for different responses. Improving the decision requires us to discover why people are acting as they are.

## Questions to carry forward

- How does my best response depend on what others do?
- Which motives or beliefs could explain the same visible behavior?
- Can this group reveal disagreement and use information that only one member holds?

Influence often happens without anyone planning it. Part V turns to deliberate persuasion and to the conversations through which people check whether they have understood one another.
